paragraphs.text: On Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. How beautiful is the sequence of good things! How sweet the succession of joy! For see, we receive feast upon feast and grace upon grace. Yesterday the Master of all entertained us; today, he who [?]

[?] …this one put off his humanity for His sake. He went into the cave of this life for us; this one came out of the cave for Him. He was wrapped in swaddling clothes for us; this one was stoned for Him. He destroyed death; this one trampled on death as it lay fallen. But let us too, brothers, run together in our discourse to the theater, to see how the great athlete contends, as he strips in the stadium of confession against the wicked adversary of human life. For truly, in Paul's words, the great Stephen became a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men. He was the first to bind on the crown of confession, the first to open the way in for the choir of martyrs, the first to resist sin to the point of blood. And it seems to me that the whole army of beings above the world, all the myriads of angels, both those who minister and those who stand in attendance, whatever honored ranks we hear of in the realm above, among principalities and powers and thrones and authorities and dominions, and the whole heavenly assembly, all made the athlete their spectacle then, as he grappled with his antagonist. Human life was spread out like a stadium for the contestants, and the two rushed at one another: the wicked adversary of human life, trained by his victory over mankind from the fall of the first-formed down to the time of Stephen, and the great contender for the faith, who counted the adversary's onset as nothing. Each had his weapons against the other: the inventor of death had the threat of death, and the disciple of life had the confession of faith. Who would not admire this new kind of contest, in which truth was decided by life and death, and death became the proof of truth? For the herald of the hidden faith and the unknown life proclaimed his message to men by deed: his readiness to leave this life was proof, to those who judge rightly, that he was exchanging it for a more precious life than the one he left behind. But it would be good to paint the contest precisely in words, as on a panel, so that the order of the wonders may be displayed to us step by step through the sequence of events. For just then the violent wind from above had scattered all the aerial and deceitful power of the demons and filled the house of the apostles; and the Spirit, divided into tongues like fire, came upon each one, according to the number of those receiving the grace. And now, at the marvel of the wonder of voice and tongue, amazement had seized those from every nation who were staying in Jerusalem, and confusion too, since people divided into many different kinds of languages had all at once come to share one tongue with the disciples. For it was not from prior training or any practice, but from the inspiration

of the Spirit, as this grace was poured all at once upon the apostles, that the power of speech came to them. For those who had broken up their common speech at the building of the earthly tower had to come into common speech again at the spiritual building of the Church. And for this reason the dispensation of the grace of the Holy Spirit fittingly begins here: so as to distribute this benefit, common to all mankind, into every kind of human speech, so that the preaching of godliness might not be shut up in a single language and remain ineffective and inoperative for those of other tongues. Now then, the Pharisees disbelieved even their own ears and mocked those who were amazed at the wonder as being deluded, as though new wine had produced such derangement in them. Peter, with a single cast of his discourse, netted three thousand souls for Christ, and from then on the Church kept growing into a multitude by the addition of those being saved. And the man lame from birth in turn opened the Beautiful Gate of the temple to those being saved: sitting beside the miracle of his own healing, he led by the hand to faith those who were lame in soul. So, as many were streaming to the preaching of the faith, and the need called for more hands among those ministering to grace, Stephen, great in wisdom and grace, is then called by the Spirit to assist the apostles. And let no one suppose, from the name of diaconate, that he ranked below the apostolic dignity. For Paul too knows himself as a minister of the mysteries of Christ; and the Lord of all, who brought about human salvation through the flesh, was not ashamed of the name of service, saying that He was in their midst as one who serves, He who works the varieties of ministries, as the Apostle says. For just as fire, once it seizes suitable material, lifts its flame on high and makes its brightness more conspicuous, so the Holy Spirit, coming into the greatness of Stephen's nature, made the rays of grace more manifest. Therefore everyone who had any share of knowledge and learning looked to him; and those who seemed to excel the rest packed themselves together in groups, as though into phalanxes, and so tried to withstand Stephen's assault. But he was equally invincible to all, engaging single-handed with many and with few. In this contest, to outward view, it was Alexandrians and Libertines and Cyrenians and men from everywhere who were grappling with the contender for truth; but the one perceived through what was visible was the father of lies, raising himself up through human faces against the truth spoken in Stephen. Yet truth triumphed over falsehood, as the champion nobly routed all the front-line fighters of deceit; and the minister of truth was plotted against by the enemy

[?] of truth, as though he were not revealing the truth that is, but fabricating a truth that is not. 'Why do you contrive these things against the herald?' I would say to the devil. 'If you have any power, harm the truth that is in Stephen. But if that truth is higher than your machinations, why do you busy your malice with the vessel of truth, destroying the container and leaving what lies within?' This is what dogs do, snapping at the stones with which they are pelted, [?]. Since the Wicked One could find no other champion of deceit, because everyone was looking toward the manifestation of truth, he remembers his own wrestling move and divides his energy between the accusers and the judges. Being present in both, he led the one group to speak lies against Stephen, and the other to receive the slander with anger. And having sown himself in various ways among the Jews, he becomes everything to Stephen: accuser and judge and executioner and all the rest of the apparatus of death, not knowing what a fall he would be thrown down with after such a verdict against Stephen. For just as skilled athletes get under the bodies of their opponents and, by some technical agility, contrive a harder fall for them, so too the great Stephen, bent to the ground, dealt the adversary a grievous crushing. For from this begins the apostles' course to the whole inhabited world; this is the beginning of the spread of the word everywhere. Had the Jewish populace not raged against the apostles in the bloody murder of Stephen, the grace of the Gospel might perhaps have been shut up in Jerusalem alone. But now, persecuted by the Jews, they were scattered, one here and another there, among the nations of the world, driving out the devil everywhere through the teaching of the mysteries. Thus Samaria receives the word; thus the eunuch's salvation is accomplished by Philip as a by-product of a journey; thus Paul, the great vessel of the Church, who had been armed by the devil with rage and threats, turns the darts against the warrior himself, banishing him from the whole world, so as to leave no place untrodden by faith in Christ. From there the word, running through the world, brings to the faith Egyptians, Syrians, Parthians and Mesopotamians, Italians and Galatians, Illyrians, Macedonians, and the nations from every quarter. Do you see Stephen's athletic skill? With how many falls the adversary was crushed, who had thought that by slander he had got the better of his opponent! But let us return again to the stadium. With what words do the slanderers stir up the people? 'He does not stop,' they say, 'speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law; for we have heard

him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.' Such, then, is the accusation of the devil's orators. And what is the folly of those who heard it? What in the accused makes them angry? What wickedness did they detect in what was said? For the charges brought against him concerned things that would happen later. They claimed he had said that the place would be destroyed and the ordinances of Moses changed. What wrong is there in this, whether he speaks truly or falsely? If he is lying, the grievous thing will not happen; if he is telling the truth, what wrong does a word do that foretells the outcome? For what is to happen will surely come about whether we are silent or not; and what remedy for the grievous things does the murder of the one who foretold them bring? Then again, it is Jesus of Nazareth who is accused, yet the sentence of punishment falls on Stephen. And yet, if it is the wrongdoer who arouses anger, and the wrong is the alteration of the place and the customs, and the accuser says that these things are being done not by Stephen but by Jesus, then the court ought surely to have been roused against the one accused. O the unjust verdict of the hearers! 'Since Jesus,' they say, 'will change the laws, let Stephen be stoned!' But how will Jesus destroy the law, when He stands toward the law as He does? He laid down every command to confirm the ancient ones; He said, 'I did not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it'; He confirmed the law against murder by teaching His disciples not even to be angry in the first place; He cut out adultery together with desire; by commanding us not to retaliate against one who has done us harm, He made it law not even to start unjust violence; by the sharing of possessions He banished the passion of greed. How, then, was none of this either mentioned or examined at the trial? I wish the council of those bloodthirsty judges were here before me now, so that I might ask them about the places for which they rage: where is that renowned temple, where are those stones of incredible size, where is that gold almost equal in weight to all the rest of the material in the temple, where are the lawful sacrifices: the ram, the calf, the lamb, the heifer, the dove, the turtledove, the scapegoat? If they condemned Stephen to death so that none of those dismal things should come to pass, let them show what they preserved for themselves by the murder. But if none of the things for whose sake that verdict was passed still exists, let them tell us: what was the murder for? But let us see, in what follows of the contest, how he who is buried under a snowstorm of stones defends himself against the murderers, and what shots he sends back against those hurling their missiles of stone. Let the children of the Jews learn the weapons of Christians, which the great Stephen used to defend himself against those who wronged him, making his deed a law for our life. For they, standing in a circle around the saint with a beastly, savage frenzy, all looked to a single target, making everything that came to hand

a weapon against Stephen. But he, like a priest offering a pure sacrifice according to the spiritual law, offering not another's body but his own, and pouring out his blood in place of the libation, through himself propitiated God, whom he saw in the heavenly sanctuary, on behalf of those who were sinning. He repaid their bloodshed with kindness, crying out in the murderers' hearing, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.' And while he was blotting out by prayer the sin that the murderers were writing out with their lawless hands, they were provoked even by the prayer, and did not stop throwing until the great Stephen, as though showered with soft flowers or some light dew, lay down into the sweet and blessed sleep. But victory has outrun the contest, and we see the crowned victor before the struggles. For before beholding the contest, we have been carried by the discourse to the end of the struggles. Yet we must not, I think, pass over in our discourse the things by which above all the martyr's virtue was displayed: what the council of murderers was like, and how the rage for murder was roused equally in all; how great was the agreement in evil among those gathered; what each one's look was, what his bearing, what was happening to his teeth, as divine Scripture indicates, that they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him. And standing in the midst of such men, and so many, and rising up against all the opposing power at work in the murderers, he prevailed over everything by the greatness of his mind, setting long-suffering against anger, disdain against threats, contempt for life against the fear of death, love against hatred, goodwill against hostility, and the revealing of truth against slander. For the contender for truth was not shown victor in one way only; but, distributing himself through manifold virtue against every form of wickedness then at work in the Jews, he grappled with all of them and overcame all. So too, I hear, in the athletic games those of superior strength often strip for the entire program of the stadium and carry off the prizes against all their opponents. Such was the leader of the martyrs' stadium, who arrayed himself against the whole power of the adversary and is proclaimed glorious in his victory over all. For the falsely named wisdom, which wrestled with him through the Libertines and Cyrenians and the wise men from Alexander's city, he defeated by true wisdom; fear by boldness; threats by disdain; bitterness by doing good; falsehood by truth. They were looking to murder, and were already arming their hands with stones, and by their looks, their panting and the gnashing of their teeth were signaling their bitterness [?]

[?] 'Men, brothers and fathers,' he says, 'hear me.' They were plausibly weaving together their slander; but to him the council of murderers was a school of truth. He did not cut his speech short from fear, nor did he grow slack at the prospect of dangers, nor did he look to death; but, keeping his soul on high and disregarding everything at his feet, he tutored them with his words like children foolishly raving, using the very things they themselves believed to prove that they had gone astray in their doctrines. Abraham is brought into the speech, and his whole story is set before their eyes in a few words; then the succession of the saints who followed. After these comes Moses: born, raised, educated, initiated on the mountain, scourging Egypt, saving Israel, foretelling the mystery of the Lord. This above all stirs up the council and inflames their sickness: that Moses too, for whom they pretended to be so zealous, was shown to be an advocate of the doctrine. At this they rose up and brought about an end worthy both of their own bitterness and of Stephen's desire. For he went beyond nature, and even before leaving the body he sees with pure eyes the heavenly gates opening for him, and what is within the sanctuary shining through: the divine glory itself and the radiance of the glory. Of the Father's glory no form is sketched in the account; but the radiance is beheld by the athlete in the form in which it appeared to men, appearing in the way that human nature could receive it. So he, having passed beyond human nature and been transformed into angelic grace, so that he was a marvel even to the murderers, since the appearance of his face had been changed to the dignity of the angels, both saw what cannot be seen and cried aloud the grace that had appeared to him. But they stopped their ears and would not accept the account of the vision; in this at least, of all things, they did well, for profane ears were not worthy to receive the account of a divine manifestation. He, then, shared the grace with those present, setting forth for all in his account the things of which he alone had been deemed worthy, saying, 'I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.' But they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed upon him with one accord. The narrative about them did well to add the cry to their deeds, to show that their choice was akin to that of the Sodomites. For their lawlessness too was called a cry by the Judge: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah,' He says, 'has come up to me.' So these men too cried out, so that their cry against Stephen might also be heard. Yet the athlete was well aware that he was being benefited by the bitterness of the murderers. For [?]

crowned by the ring of those stoning him all around, he received what was happening as a victor's crown woven in the hands of his enemies. Therefore he repays the murderers with blessing, not thinking it right that what was done to him should be divided into opposite outcomes, bringing life to him and destruction to his opponents; rather, he wished that his enemies too, as having helped to cause his good fortune, should not fall short of what he himself had been granted. This is how one who sees Christ knows to treat those who make war on him. For since he saw the lawgiver of long-suffering, he remembered the laws that command us to love our enemies, to do good to those who hate us, and to pray for those who make war on us. But the athlete is not glorified by human praises. For the aim of his contest did not look to glory from men; rather, surpassing the whole world by the greatness of his achievement, he also outran the measures of human power, casting every power of encomium behind him. So let him hold the victory over every human word; but let him, through his story, contend alongside us for the salvation of souls. For just as among bodily athletes those who have retired from the contests train the young in athletic exercises, teaching them by some technical agility to slip the holds of their opponents, so I think we too must be trained in godliness by the great Stephen, so that through him we may escape the holds of the Pneumatomachians. For those who rage against the glory of the Spirit claim that Stephen is an advocate of their absurdity, since, gazing into heaven, he saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. So, to overthrow the doctrines of godliness, they say: 'If the Spirit must by all means be numbered with the Father and the Son, how is it that Stephen did not see the Spirit too with the Son in his vision?' How, then, will Stephen stretch out his hand to those who are tripped up by such arguments? How will he set upright by his wrestling skill those whose knees are buckling? Indeed, the help that overturns the unbelief of the opponent is right here. You ask, O fighter against the Spirit: 'If the glory of the Father was seen, and the Son standing at the right hand, where is the Spirit?' If the Spirit were in you, you would not have passed over the word about Him that lies before you, just as the blind pass by gold lying at their feet without knowing it. But now at least listen, unless, like the Jews, you are stopping your ears. How did Stephen see the glory above the heavens? Who opened the gates of heaven for him? Was the achievement a work of human power? Was it some angel who lifted the nature lying below to that height? It is not so. For this is not what the narrative about him says, but that Stephen, being great in the [?]

[?]… power, or having been filled with angelic help, that he saw what he saw? But what does Scripture say? “But Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit, saw the glory of God” and the only-begotten Son of God. For, as the Prophet says, light cannot be seen unless it is beheld in light: “For in your light,” he says, “we shall see light.” It is impossible, then, to contemplate light except in light. How could anyone gaze at the sun while standing outside its rays? And the Only-begotten Light is beheld in the light of the Father, that is, in the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him. For this reason Stephen, first illuminated by the glory of the Spirit, comes to apprehend the glory of the Father and of the Son. Otherwise, how shall we say that the Gospel's declaration is true, that “no one has ever seen God”? And how shall we say that the Apostle does not contradict the narrative when he says, “whom no human being has seen or can see”? For if the glory of the Father and of the Son had become something human nature and power could contain, then the one who declared the divine vision beyond human capacity would surely be false. Yet it must be that he does not lie and that the narrative is true. So the villainy of the Pneumatomachians, the fighters against the Spirit, is plainly exposed, since Scripture testifies that like is beheld by like. For Stephen does not see the Divine while remaining in human nature and power. Rather, blended with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he was lifted up through the Spirit to the understanding of God. So if without the Spirit no one can even say “Lord Jesus,” as the Apostle says, nor comprehend the Father's glory, it has been clearly shown that where the Spirit is, there the Son too is beheld and the Father's glory apprehended. But the fighters against Christ throw up against us another weapon of impiety drawn from the narrative. They say that it signifies the inferiority of the Only-begotten, for they take his standing at the right hand of the Father as proof that he is subject to the Father's authority. What, then, would I say to them about Paul? And what about the prophet David before him, both of whom set forth the glory of the Only-begotten by the teaching of the Spirit? For David says, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” And the Apostle says that the Lord has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. If, then, standing is a sign of inferiority, sitting is surely a sign of equal honor. So let them either strike out the testimonies that befit God, by which the exaltation of the right hand is signified, or else accept this one reverently as well. For in each of the cases mentioned there is one teacher, the grace of the Spirit. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, both saw what he saw and spoke what he saw. David calls him Lord in the Spirit, as the Gospel says. And Paul, as he himself says, speaks mysteries in the Spirit. If, then, the teacher is one, and has no disagreement with himself

(for the teacher is the Spirit of truth who dwells in those who are borne by God), how could anyone suspect some disagreement in the doctrines? “But,” our opponent says, “sitting and standing indicate different meanings, as they are commonly understood.” I say so too. But what the force of these words shows in the case of bodies, it is not reverent to reckon the same for the incorporeal nature. In a human being, sitting describes the placing of the body on the hips, so that the knee is not strained continually by bearing the body's weight on its own. Conversely, standing means that a person is upright on the knees and is not resting on the hips by sitting. But in the case of the transcendent nature, sitting and standing are both free of such notions, and each is equally removed from the meaning ordinarily understood. For we shall not take standing on the knee to belong to the incorporeal, nor sitting on the hips to belong to what has no shape. Rather, through each word we shall reverently understand what is steadfast in every good and unchangeable in every respect. The one who says that the Divine stands and the one who says that it sits do not differ from each other in meaning at all, despite the difference of words. The one teaches that the Divine is firmly set in the good, the other that it is immovably established there. The prophet David and the apostle Paul, each recounting in his own words the sitting of the Only-begotten, did not give us to understand that the Son is seated while the Father stands, even though they mention only the Son's sitting. In the same way, when you hear in Stephen's case of the Son's standing, you could no longer reasonably suppose that the Father is sitting. For as with Paul and David the Father's sitting is acknowledged along with the Son's sitting at his right hand, though the text had taught nothing beforehand about the Father, so too with Stephen the Son's standing indicates the same about the glory of the Father. For only thus would the principle of the image be preserved: if whatever is understood and beheld in it is believed to be the same in the archetype as well. As the archetypal beauty is expressed in the image through its own features, good in the good, light in the light, and so in all things, so too in the Son's sitting, whatever that word gives us to understand, the Father's sitting is also apprehended, and likewise standing in standing. Thus the principle of the image does not break down by becoming estranged from the properties of the archetype. Let this, brothers, be our reflection in passing on the question before us, since Stephen's vision brought such a reflection into our discourse. And may it be granted to us not only to be spectators of Stephen's contest but also sharers in his grace, filled with the Holy Spirit, for the overthrow of our adversaries and for the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory [?]
